hero.headline: Federal decision looms on Fort Pierce's rare deep-sea coral reef as activists push to preserve protections
hero.body:
A rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth, located just off the coast of Fort Pierce, faces an uncertain future as federal officials prepare to make a final decision on proposals that would reopen parts of the protected area to shrimp trawling. Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County to rally support for the Oculina Bank, a reef that thrives hundreds of feet below the surface in deep, dark waters and provides habitat for more than 2,000 marine species.

The federally-appointed South Atlantic Marine Fishery Council voted in January to reopen more than 24 square nautical miles of the reef to shrimp trawling, an area larger than the island of Manhattan. The decision came despite tens of thousands of petition signatures opposing the move and warnings from scientists that trawling destroyed as much as 90 percent of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the rare reef, said the coral provides essential habitat and food for fish populations. Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, expressed devastation at the council's vote, noting it was the same body that decades ago approved protecting the reef.

Unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive, the Oculina Bank lives in deep, dark waters. Perry and Gilmore were among scientists who spoke at the gathering, urging the public to help save the reef. Gilmore emphasized that corals are in trouble worldwide and that no more should be destroyed. The coral grows very slowly and has been present for a long time, Perry said.

The proposal now sits with NOAA, which will make the final decision. The federal agency is expected to release draft rules within the coming months, giving the public one more opportunity to weigh in before officials decide whether to move forward. Activists are urging residents to write letters to their congressmen and to those who might influence the decisions on protecting the coral.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie daughter charged with attempted murder after setting fire with mother trapped inside bedroom
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman faces attempted murder and arson charges after allegedly setting fire to a bedroom door Sunday night while a 62-year-old woman was trapped inside the room. Michelle Picard, 26, was arrested following the incident that occurred around 9:05 p.m. in the 1500 block of Southeast Airoso Boulevard.

According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, the victim first noticed smoke coming from underneath her bedroom door and discovered Picard standing nearby when she opened it. When the victim attempted to retrieve a fire extinguisher, Picard allegedly physically attacked her and tried to prevent her from putting out the fire. Police say Picard made threatening statements and attempted to push the victim toward the flames. The victim managed to escape to a bathroom, lock the door, and call 911. During the emergency call, Picard could be heard banging on the bathroom door in the background.

Officers and St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded to the scene, evacuated everyone safely, and detained Picard outside the residence. She resisted arrest, causing injuries to one officer's leg and requiring another officer to receive treatment for smoke inhalation. Both officers were treated at a local hospital and released. The victim was also hospitalized for injuries sustained during the incident. Fire investigators from multiple agencies, including the State Fire Marshal's Office, determined the blaze was intentionally set.

Picard was taken to a hospital for medical evaluation before being cleared and transported to jail. She faces charges of attempted murder, arson and resisting arrest without violence, with a total bond amount of $510,000. The fire damaged the residence, and the American Red Cross is assisting the victim with temporary housing. Police emphasized this was an isolated domestic incident with no ongoing threat to the community.

cards.headline: School bus driver arrested in Treasure Coast after second student makes allegations
cards.body:

The driver was taken into custody after law enforcement reviewed the allegations brought forward by the second student. The case represents an escalation from an earlier investigation that began with a single student report.

School transportation officials are reviewing their safety protocols in response to the arrest. The investigation remains active as authorities work to determine the full scope of the allegations and whether additional students may have been affected.

Parents with students who ride school buses in the area are being encouraged to speak with their children about any concerns. The school district continues to cooperate with law enforcement as the investigation proceeds.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman charged with attempted murder after setting bedroom on fire with mother inside
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman is facing attempted murder and arson charges after allegedly setting fire to a bedroom door while a 62-year-old woman was trapped inside the room Sunday night. Port St. Lucie police responded to reports of a domestic disturbance and active house fire around 9:05 p.m. in the 1500 block of Southeast Airoso Boulevard.

According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, the victim first noticed smoke coming from underneath her bedroom door and discovered Michelle Picard, 26, standing nearby when she opened it. When the victim attempted to retrieve a fire extinguisher, Picard allegedly physically attacked her and tried to prevent her from putting out the fire. Police say Picard made threatening statements and attempted to push the victim toward the flames. The victim managed to escape to a bathroom, lock the door, and call 911. During the emergency call, Picard could be heard banging on the bathroom door in the background.

Officers found Picard outside the residence and detained her. She resisted arrest, causing injuries to one officer's leg and requiring another officer to receive treatment for smoke inhalation. Both officers were treated at a local hospital and released. The victim was also hospitalized for treatment of injuries sustained during the incident. Picard was taken to a hospital for medical evaluation before being cleared and transported to jail.

Fire investigators from the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Criminal Investigations Division, Crime Scene Investigators, St. Lucie County Fire District, and the State Fire Marshal's Office determined the blaze was intentionally set. Picard faces charges of attempted murder, arson and resisting arrest without violence. Her total bond amount is $510,000. The American Red Cross is assisting the victim with temporary housing and support services. Police emphasized this was an isolated domestic incident and there is no ongoing threat to the community.

cards.headline: Body of suspect recovered after double homicide at Vero Beach library
cards.body:
The body of a suspect who fled into the ocean after killing two people at a Vero Beach library has been recovered, according to authorities. The suspect killed his wife and another man at the library before escaping into the water.

The incident took place at a Vero Beach library, where the violent attack left two people dead. After the killings, the suspect fled the scene and entered the ocean. Law enforcement launched a search operation to locate him.

Authorities have now confirmed that the suspect's body was found. The recovery of the body brings closure to an intensive search effort that followed the deadly attack. The incident represents one of the most serious violent crimes to occur in the Vero Beach area in recent memory.

The investigation into the double homicide continues as authorities work to understand the full circumstances of the attack. The library shooting has shaken the local community, which relies on the facility as a public gathering space and resource center.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff arrests three in retail theft ring that hit Stuart and Fort Pierce hardware stores
cards.teaser: Operation Hammer Time resulted in arrests connected to burglaries at more than 40 hardware stores across 13 counties, including multiple locations in Stuart and Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a retail theft ring dubbed Operation Hammer Time that targeted hardware stores across Martin, St. Lucie and Palm Beach counties from December 2025 to April 2026. Major Ruben Romero said Johnny Batista, 19; Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39; and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31 were all involved in a series of burglaries that hit at least 40 stores across 13 counties. Hardware stores in Stuart, Fort Pierce, Jupiter, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach and West Palm Beach were among the locations targeted, along with stores in Broward County.

Investigators say the suspects would use a sledgehammer or other blunt object to smash the glass, completing the thefts within minutes before police arrived or alarms were triggered. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage to stores. The stolen goods were taken back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold. Batista is connected to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025.

Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. The suspects face charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Romero noted that burglaries happened before December, and investigators are still looking for one other suspect.

cards.headline: Rare Flesh-Eating Bacteria Found in Miami-Dade and Other Florida Counties, Health Officials Warn
cards.body:
State health officials have confirmed the presence of a rare flesh-eating bacteria in Florida, including in Miami-Dade County. The bacteria poses a health risk to residents across multiple Florida counties.

The bacteria identified is known to cause severe tissue infections. State health authorities issued the warning to alert Florida residents and healthcare providers about the presence of this pathogen in state waters and communities. Miami-Dade County is among the areas where the bacteria has been detected, though officials indicated it has been found in other parts of Florida as well.

Florida residents who come into contact with brackish or saltwater, particularly those with open wounds or compromised immune systems, face elevated risk from this type of bacterial infection. Health officials typically advise people with cuts or abrasions to avoid water exposure in affected areas and to seek immediate medical attention if they develop symptoms following water contact. The bacteria can cause rapidly progressing infections that require urgent medical intervention.

State health officials are working to monitor the situation and provide guidance to medical facilities across Florida. The warning serves as a reminder to residents statewide to take precautions when engaging in water activities, especially during warmer months when such bacteria are more prevalent in Florida's coastal and estuarine environments. Healthcare providers have been alerted to watch for symptoms and begin treatment quickly if infections are suspected, as early intervention is critical in cases involving this type of bacteria.

cards.headline: Vero Beach approves $190,000 sidewalk project on Iris Lane
cards.teaser: The city of Vero Beach has approved funding for a new sidewalk on Iris Lane with a price tag of $190,000.
cards.body:
Vero Beach city officials have given the green light to a $190,000 sidewalk project on Iris Lane. The approval represents a significant infrastructure investment in the community's pedestrian safety and walkability.

The Iris Lane sidewalk joins other ongoing efforts to improve pedestrian access throughout Vero Beach. City officials have been working to address gaps in the sidewalk network across various neighborhoods, making it safer for residents to walk in their communities.

The project funding will cover construction of the new sidewalk along Iris Lane. City officials will now move forward with the engineering and construction phases of the project.

cards.headline: Vero Beach honors Florida woman with new historical marker
cards.teaser: A historical marker has been installed in Vero Beach to commemorate a notable Florida woman.
cards.body:
Vero Beach recently unveiled a historical marker recognizing the contributions of a significant Florida woman. The marker adds to the community's efforts to preserve and celebrate local history.

Historical markers serve as educational tools that help residents and visitors understand the people and events that shaped their community. The new marker in Vero Beach continues this tradition of honoring those who made important contributions to the area.

The installation represents ongoing work to document and preserve Indian River County's history. Community members can visit the marker to learn more about this influential figure's role in Florida history.

cards.headline: New lifeguard watch towers arrive at Vero Beach's South Beach
cards.teaser: Two lifeguard watch towers were delivered to South Beach on a flatbed semi-truck, part of ongoing beach safety improvements.
cards.body:
A flatbed semi-truck arrived at South Beach on the afternoon of May 28 carrying two lifeguard watch towers. Chief Lifeguard David Figueredo arrived on the scene several minutes later to oversee the delivery.

The new watch towers represent an investment in beach safety infrastructure at one of the area's popular beaches. Lifeguard towers provide elevated vantage points for beach safety personnel to monitor swimmers and respond quickly to emergencies.

The delivery is part of ongoing improvements to beach facilities and safety equipment. The towers will be installed at South Beach to enhance lifeguard operations during the busy summer season.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Islamic Center marks 10 years since arson fire
cards.teaser: The Islamic Center of Fort Pierce is reflecting on a significant event from a decade ago.
cards.body:
The Islamic Center of Fort Pierce is marking the 10-year anniversary of an arson fire that occurred at the facility. The incident, which took place in 2016, was a significant event in the community's history.

The Fort Pierce Islamic Center has been part of the St. Lucie County community for years, serving local Muslim residents. The arson fire a decade ago represented a challenging moment for the congregation and the broader community.

The anniversary provides an opportunity for reflection on how the community has moved forward in the years since. The Islamic Center continues to serve as a place of worship and community gathering for local residents.

cards.headline: Jewel Collins, longtime Cocoa city councilmember, dies at 89
cards.teaser: Jewel Collins, known as the 'Queen of Cocoa' and a former city councilmember, has died at age 89.
cards.body:
Jewel Collins, a longtime Cocoa city councilmember who earned the title 'Queen of Cocoa,' has died at the age of 89. Collins was a well-known figure in Brevard County politics and community affairs.

During her time on the Cocoa City Council, Collins served the community and played a role in local government decisions affecting residents. Her long tenure in public service made her a familiar name to many in the area.

Collins' death marks the end of an era for Cocoa, where she was a prominent civic leader for many years. Her contributions to the city spanned decades of public service.

cards.headline: Martin County employee accused of identity theft targeting 87-year-old resident
cards.teaser: A county employee faces accusations of using an 87-year-old resident's personal information to make a down payment on a car.
cards.body:
An employee has been accused of using the personal information of an 87-year-old resident to put a down payment on a vehicle. The alleged identity theft involves a vulnerable senior citizen and raises concerns about the protection of residents' private information.

The case highlights the risks that elderly residents face from identity theft and financial fraud. Law enforcement is investigating the allegations against the employee.

Identity theft crimes can have serious financial and emotional impacts on victims, particularly older adults who may be less able to recover from financial losses.

cards.headline: Five hospitalized after multi-vehicle crash and fire closes I-95 in Martin County
cards.teaser: A collision Monday night on Interstate 95 northbound near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park sparked a vehicle fire and sent five people to the hospital.
cards.body:
Five people were hospitalized Monday night after a multi-vehicle crash on Interstate 95 that also sparked a vehicle fire, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The collision occurred just before 10 p.m. on I-95 northbound near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park in Stuart. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the scene, where they found one of the vehicles on fire and quickly extinguished the flames.

Two people suffered traumatic injuries and were transported to the hospital, while three others sustained minor injuries and were also taken for medical treatment. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while law enforcement investigated the crash, causing significant delays for motorists.

As of Tuesday morning, all lanes have reopened. The Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the circumstances of the crash.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman loses home and irreplaceable photos of late son in lightning strike fire
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera is displaced and calling for help after a lightning strike last month destroyed her Fort Pierce home, leaving her with heavy damage and almost nothing left.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce woman is displaced and rebuilding after a lightning strike tore through her home last month, leaving her with broken windows, heavy damage, and the loss of irreplaceable belongings. Rosa Rivera returned home from getting a haircut at church when a utility worker stopped her outside. The worker told her the house appeared to be on fire. St. Lucie County District Firefighters rushed to put out the flames, and Rivera was told a lightning strike caused the fire.

Walking into her damaged home left Rivera stunned. She lost clothes, furniture and irreplaceable personal belongings including photos of her late son, who passed away three years ago. The uninsured Rivera is now staying at her nephew's home while she rebuilds. Rivera, who is also disabled, was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home.

Despite the overwhelming losses, Rivera said she is grateful that she was not inside when the fire broke out. A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie neighborhood, officials monitoring
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before running toward nearby homes.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes, marking an unusual wildlife sighting along the Treasure Coast. The video, posted on the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Facebook page, shows the large black bear navigating through residential waters in what officials described as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear. If it does not move from the area on its own, bear biologists may set a trap to try and capture and relocate it. Port St. Lucie police stated that as Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods can occur. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions.

Wildlife officials emphasize specific protocols when encountering black bears in residential areas. If residents spot a bear, authorities recommend maintaining significant distance, never approaching the animal, and avoiding any attempts to feed it. Port St. Lucie police advise residents to keep children and pets away from bears and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food and bird seed around their properties. During unexpected bear encounters, officials stress remaining calm and avoiding running, and instead slowly backing away while keeping the bear visible.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House in Fort Pierce reopens as downtown dining destination after renovation
cards.teaser: The Boston House, a downtown Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, has officially reopened as a new dining experience.
cards.body:
A historic Fort Pierce landmark is entering a new chapter. The Boston House, a downtown staple for more than a century, has officially reopened as a new dining experience along South Indian River Drive, bringing fresh energy to a city working to redefine its future. Built in 1909, the home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served a variety of roles over the decades. Now, its newest owners are working to preserve its past while reimagining its purpose.

Originally built by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway, who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the Boston House remains closely tied to the region's early development. Co-owner Georgette Angelos said the goal is simple: make guests feel at home while honoring the building's legacy. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details, including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that nod to the home's past.

General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum downtown. Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history, blending preservation with a modern dining atmosphere. Laird said Fort Pierce has done a great job bringing new life to the downtown area, and the Boston House now stands as both a historic landmark and a renewed gathering place serving up a new chapter for the city.

hero.headline: Heiress donates land adjacent to Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve to block development
hero.body:
An heiress has purchased and donated land adjacent to the Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve in a move aimed at preventing future development in the environmentally sensitive area. The land acquisition expands protections for the preserve, which protects critical scrub habitat in northern Martin County.

The donation adds acreage to one of the region's most important natural areas. The Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve already protects rare scrub ecosystem that supports endangered species and provides essential habitat. By purchasing adjacent parcels and placing them into conservation, the heiress has blocked potential residential or commercial development that could have fragmented the habitat.

The preserve sits in Hobe Sound, where development pressure continues to mount as population growth spreads northward from Palm Beach County. Conservation groups have long identified the scrub habitat in this area as priority land for protection due to its rarity and ecological importance. The sandy soils and unique plant communities found in scrub ecosystems have been dramatically reduced across Florida as development has expanded.

The donated land will now be managed as part of the larger preserve system, ensuring permanent protection from development. This conservation strategy of purchasing threatened parcels and transferring them to public or nonprofit ownership has become increasingly common in Martin County as residents and philanthropists work to preserve the region's natural character against development pressure.

cards.headline: Indian River County restaurant inspection results include perfect score and failure
cards.teaser: One Indian River County restaurant earned a perfect inspection score while another failed its health inspection, according to recent reports.
cards.body:
Health inspectors in Indian River County recently completed restaurant inspections that resulted in dramatically different outcomes for two local establishments. One restaurant achieved a perfect score during its inspection, while another failed to meet health code standards.

The inspections are part of regular monitoring by the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, which conducts surprise visits to restaurants throughout the state. Inspectors check for proper food handling, storage temperatures, cleanliness, and other health code requirements. A perfect score indicates no violations were found during the inspection.

Restaurants that fail inspections must address violations and undergo reinspection before continuing operations. The inspection reports are public records and provide transparency for diners making choices about where to eat in Indian River County.

cards.headline: Florida mall partially demolished as redevelopment moves forward
cards.teaser: A Florida shopping mall has been partially torn down, marking the end of an era for the retail center that once drew shoppers from across the region.
cards.body:
Demolition crews have begun tearing down portions of a Florida mall, removing structures that once housed retail stores and served as a community gathering place. The partial demolition represents a significant shift in the property's future as developers prepare the site for new uses.

The mall operated for decades as a traditional enclosed shopping center during the height of indoor mall popularity. Like many similar properties across Florida and the nation, the facility faced declining foot traffic and store closures as shopping habits shifted toward online retail and open-air lifestyle centers. Multiple stores eventually closed, leaving large sections of the mall vacant.

Redevelopment of shuttered mall properties has become increasingly common across Florida as owners seek new purposes for large retail sites. The demolition clears the way for future construction on the property, though the specific plans for the site represent a new chapter for a location that holds memories for many local shoppers who visited during the mall's heyday.

cards.headline: Restaurant in NewMarket Square to open this week after delays
cards.teaser: A new restaurant facing several construction and permitting delays will finally open its doors this week in NewMarket Square shopping center.
cards.body:
A restaurant that has experienced multiple setbacks is scheduled to open this week in NewMarket Square, bringing a new dining option to the shopping center. The opening comes after the business faced several delays that pushed back its original timeline.

The delays are common in restaurant construction and permitting, where building modifications, equipment installation, and final inspections can extend opening dates beyond initial projections. Restaurant operators must complete multiple steps including health inspections, fire safety checks, and final permit approvals before serving their first customers.

The opening adds to dining choices available at NewMarket Square, a retail center that serves local residents. New restaurant openings typically draw strong initial interest from community members eager to try new food options in their area.

cards.teaser: The Texas-based convenience store chain known for massive facilities and clean bathrooms is planning locations in six additional states.
cards.body:
Buc-ee's, the popular convenience store chain famous for its oversized facilities and highway travel amenities, has announced plans to expand into six new states. The company continues its aggressive growth strategy beyond its Texas roots and existing southeastern locations.

Buc-ee's builds massive travel centers that feature dozens of fuel pumps, extensive food options, and exceptionally clean restrooms. The stores have developed a cult following among road travelers and have become destinations rather than just stops. Each location employs significant numbers of workers and draws travelers from surrounding areas.

The expansion includes plans for Arizona locations in the near future. Buc-ee's typically builds along major interstate corridors where high traffic volumes can support the large-format stores. The company's growth has made it a notable presence in states where it opens, often drawing crowds of curious customers when new locations debut.

cards.headline: Florida residents invited to vote for best burrito restaurant
cards.teaser: A poll asks Floridians to weigh in on which restaurant serves the best burritos in their area.
cards.body:
Florida restaurant customers can participate in a poll to determine which establishment serves the best burritos in town. The voting campaign invites residents to share their opinions about their favorite burrito spots across the state.

Burrito restaurants have proliferated across Florida in recent years, ranging from national chains to local independent establishments. The variety includes traditional Mexican taquerias, fast-casual chains, and fusion concepts that put creative spins on the wrapped format. Competition for customer loyalty has intensified as more options have opened.

Reader polls about best restaurants generate engagement from food enthusiasts eager to support their preferred establishments and discover new options. The results often highlight lesser-known local favorites alongside popular chains, giving diners insight into community preferences.

cards.headline: Two Tallahassee restaurants recognized in Michelin Guide
cards.teaser: A pair of Tallahassee dining establishments have earned spots in the prestigious Michelin Guide, bringing recognition to the capital city's food scene.
cards.body:
Two restaurants in Tallahassee have been included in the Michelin Guide, marking a significant achievement for the establishments and the city's culinary reputation. The Michelin Guide is one of the most respected restaurant rating systems in the world, and inclusion represents recognition of quality and excellence.

The Michelin Guide has expanded its coverage across the United States in recent years, reviewing restaurants in more cities beyond its traditional focus areas. Being selected for the guide, even without a star rating, indicates that inspectors found the restaurants worthy of mention and recommendation to travelers and food enthusiasts.

For Tallahassee's dining scene, the recognition brings visibility and prestige that can attract food-focused visitors to the capital city. Restaurants included in the guide often see increased interest from diners seeking elevated experiences and from culinary professionals who follow industry recognition.

cards.headline: Florida legislature advances expanded homestead property tax exemption for state ballot
cards.teaser: Florida lawmakers have approved placing a constitutional amendment on the ballot that would expand the homestead property tax exemption for residents across the state, including Treasure Coast counties.
cards.body:
The Florida legislature has approved a measure that will send a constitutional amendment to voters expanding the homestead property tax exemption. The proposal would allow Florida homeowners to claim larger exemptions on their primary residences, potentially reducing annual property tax bills for residents across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

The constitutional amendment must be approved by voters in a statewide referendum before taking effect. If passed, the expanded exemption would provide tax relief to homeowners but could also reduce revenue flowing to county governments, school districts, and municipalities that rely on property taxes to fund services.

Local government officials in Treasure Coast counties will be watching the ballot measure closely, as its passage could require adjustments to municipal and county budgets. The exact impact on local services would depend on how many homeowners claim the expanded exemption and the overall assessed property values in each jurisdiction.

hero.headline: Rare Flesh-Eating Bacteria Found in Miami-Dade and Other Florida Counties, Health Officials Warn
hero.body:
State health officials have confirmed the presence of a rare flesh-eating bacteria in Florida, including in Miami-Dade County. The bacteria poses a health risk to residents across multiple Florida counties.

The bacteria identified is known to cause severe tissue infections. State health authorities issued the warning to alert Florida residents and healthcare providers about the presence of this pathogen in state waters and communities. Miami-Dade County is among the areas where the bacteria has been detected, though officials indicated it has been found in other parts of Florida as well.

Florida residents who come into contact with brackish or saltwater, particularly those with open wounds or compromised immune systems, face elevated risk from this type of bacterial infection. Health officials typically advise people with cuts or abrasions to avoid water exposure in affected areas and to seek immediate medical attention if they develop symptoms following water contact. The bacteria can cause rapidly progressing infections that require urgent medical intervention.

State health officials are working to monitor the situation and provide guidance to medical facilities across Florida. The warning serves as a reminder to residents statewide to take precautions when engaging in water activities, especially during warmer months when such bacteria are more prevalent in Florida's coastal and estuarine environments. Healthcare providers have been alerted to watch for symptoms and begin treatment quickly if infections are suspected, as early intervention is critical in cases involving this type of bacteria.

cards.body:

Florida established one of the nation's most ambitious wildlife corridor systems to allow animals to move between habitat areas without encountering deadly roads or development barriers. The corridor approach helps maintain genetic diversity in wildlife populations and allows species to adapt to changing environmental conditions. Florida's large-scale implementation provides real-world data on how corridor systems function and benefit both wildlife and human communities.

Research related to the Florida corridor system suggests that climate change could intensify the importance of connected habitats. The research indicates climate change could amplify swings between quiet periods and hyperactive seasons, making adaptable wildlife populations more critical. If Florida's model expands nationally, it could reshape conservation strategy across the country and help wildlife populations cope with environmental pressures.

hero.headline: Five hospitalized after multi-vehicle crash and fire shuts down I-95 in Martin County
hero.body:
Five people were injured Monday night after a multi-vehicle collision on Interstate 95 in Martin County that sparked a vehicle fire and shut down all northbound lanes for hours. The crash occurred just before 10 p.m. on northbound I-95 near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park, prompting a major emergency response.

Martin County Fire Rescue crews arrived to find one of the vehicles engulfed in flames and quickly extinguished the fire. Two people suffered traumatic injuries and were transported to area hospitals, while three others sustained minor injuries and were also taken for medical treatment. The extent of their current conditions has not been disclosed.

All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while law enforcement investigated the circumstances of the crash. The closure caused significant traffic delays for drivers traveling through Stuart during the late evening hours. By Tuesday morning, all lanes had reopened to traffic.

The Florida Highway Patrol is handling the investigation into what caused the multi-vehicle collision. The crash is one of several serious incidents on Interstate 95 in Martin County in recent months, highlighting ongoing safety concerns on the heavily traveled corridor that connects communities throughout the Treasure Coast.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office arrests three in retail theft ring that hit Stuart and regional hardware stores
cards.teaser: A multi-county investigation dubbed Operation Hammer Time led to arrests in a theft ring that burglarized at least 40 hardware stores, including locations in Stuart, stealing roughly $500,000 worth of property.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a major retail theft operation that targeted hardware stores across the Treasure Coast and South Florida over a five-month period. Major Ruben Romero said Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31, were involved in a series of burglaries at hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties from December 2025 to April 2026. At least 40 stores across 13 counties were burglarized, with the stolen goods taken back to Miami-Dade County where the suspects lived to be sold.

According to the Sheriff's Office, hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce and Jupiter were targeted. The crews used a sledgehammer or other blunt object to smash the glass and often completed the thefts within minutes, before police arrived or alarms were triggered. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage to stores. Investigators connected Batista to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025.

Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and is being held in Martin County Jail, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. Major Romero said the thefts have a broader impact on the community beyond the immediate losses. The suspects are facing charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Investigators say there are burglaries that happened before December and they are still looking for one other suspect.

cards.headline: Activists rally in Martin County to save rare deep-sea coral reef off Fort Pierce from shrimp trawling
cards.teaser: Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library after a federally appointed council voted to roll back protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth and home to more than 2,000 marine species.
cards.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County to rally for the protection of the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef located just off the coast of Fort Pierce. Unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive, the Oculina Bank thrives in deep, dark waters hundreds of feet below the surface and is found nowhere else on Earth. The reef is home to more than 2,000 marine species and provides critical habitat and food sources for fish populations.

Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the rare reef, and Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, urged the public to help save the reef at the gathering. Despite calls from scientists and activists to reject the proposal, in January the federally appointed South Atlantic Marine Fishery Council voted to reopen more than 24 square nautical miles of the reef, an area larger than the island of Manhattan, to shrimp trawling. Scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago.

The proposal is now with NOAA, who will make the final decision. The agency is expected to release draft rules within the coming months, giving the public one more opportunity to weigh in before officials decide whether to move forward. Activists are encouraging residents to write letters to their congressman and those who might be able to influence the decisions. Perry said he was devastated that the same council that decades ago approved protecting the reef now wants to amend that protection and open it up to destructive fishing efforts.

hero.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie's Town Park community
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before running toward nearby homes.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes, marking an unusual wildlife sighting along the Treasure Coast. The video, posted on the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Facebook page, shows the large black bear navigating through residential waters in what officials described as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear. If it does not move from the area on its own, bear biologists may set a trap to try and capture and relocate it. Port St. Lucie police stated on Facebook that as Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods can occur. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions, making Tuesday's Port St. Lucie encounter particularly noteworthy for local residents.

Wildlife officials emphasize specific protocols when encountering black bears in residential areas. If residents spot a bear, authorities recommend maintaining significant distance, never approaching the animal, and avoiding any attempts to feed it. Port St. Lucie police advise residents to keep children and pets away from bears and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties. During unexpected bear encounters, officials stress remaining calm and avoiding running. Instead, residents should slowly back away while keeping the bear visible, speak in calm, firm tones, and ensure the animal has a clear escape route.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman loses home and irreplaceable belongings after lightning strike causes fire
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera was displaced after a lightning strike tore through her Fort Pierce home last month, leaving her with broken windows, heavy damage, and the loss of photos of her late son.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce woman is displaced and calling for help after a lightning strike tore through her home, leaving her with broken windows, heavy damage, and almost nothing left. Last month, Rosa Rivera returned home from getting a haircut at church when a utility worker stopped her outside. When she returned home, the utility worker told her he thought her house was on fire. St. Lucie County District Firefighters rushed to put out the flames. Rivera was told a lightning strike caused the fire.

Rivera lost clothes, furniture and irreplaceable personal belongings including photos of her late son who passed away three years ago. Walking into her damaged home left her stunned. The damage left Rivera displaced. She is uninsured and is now staying at her nephew's home while she rebuilds.

Rivera, who is also disabled, was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home. A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced. Despite everything, Rivera said she is holding onto gratitude that she was not inside when the fire broke out. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House reopens as downtown Fort Pierce dining destination
cards.teaser: The Boston House, a downtown Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909, has officially reopened as a new dining experience, bringing fresh energy to the city's revitalized downtown.
cards.body:
A historic Fort Pierce landmark is entering a new chapter. The Boston House, a downtown staple for more than a century, has officially reopened as a new dining experience, bringing fresh energy to a city working to redefine its future. Built in 1909 along South Indian River Drive, the home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served a variety of roles over the decades. Now, its newest owners are working to preserve its past while reimagining its purpose.

Co-owner Georgette Angelos described Fort Pierce as eclectic, artistic, with deep, beautiful history. Behind its historic doors, the goal is simple: make guests feel at home while honoring the building's legacy. Originally built by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway, who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the Boston House remains closely tied to the region's early development. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details, including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that nod to the home's past.

General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum downtown. Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history, blending preservation with a modern dining atmosphere. The Boston House now stands as both a historic landmark and a renewed gathering place serving up a new chapter for downtown Fort Pierce.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman charged with attempted murder after setting bedroom on fire with mother inside
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman is facing attempted murder and arson charges after allegedly setting fire to a bedroom door while a 62-year-old woman was trapped inside the room Sunday night. Port St. Lucie police responded to reports of a domestic disturbance and active house fire around 9:05 p.m. in the 1500 block of Southeast Airoso Boulevard.

According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, the victim first noticed smoke coming from underneath her bedroom door and discovered Michelle Picard, 26, standing nearby when she opened it. When the victim attempted to retrieve a fire extinguisher, Picard allegedly physically attacked her and tried to prevent her from putting out the fire. Police say Picard made threatening statements and attempted to push the victim toward the flames. The victim managed to escape to a bathroom, lock the door, and call 911. During the emergency call, Picard could be heard banging on the bathroom door in the background.

Officers found Picard outside the residence and detained her. She resisted arrest, causing injuries to one officer's leg and requiring another officer to receive treatment for smoke inhalation. Both officers were treated at a local hospital and released. The victim was also hospitalized for treatment of injuries sustained during the incident. Picard was taken to a hospital for medical evaluation before being cleared and transported to jail.

Fire investigators from the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Criminal Investigations Division, Crime Scene Investigators, St. Lucie County Fire District, and the State Fire Marshal's Office determined the blaze was intentionally set. Picard faces charges of attempted murder, arson and resisting arrest without violence. Her total bond amount is $510,000. The American Red Cross is assisting the victim with temporary housing and support services. Police emphasized this was an isolated domestic incident and there is no ongoing threat to the community.
